events.title: Israel sets out with all he has for Beersheba
events.narrative_summary: Israel sets out with everything that belongs to him and comes to Beersheba.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 46:1 follows at once on Israel's resolve to go (45:28), so the journey starts at the end of that event. The text gives no starting point and no duration; Hebron (Gen 37:14) to Beersheba is about 50 km by road, and an army-mode caravan with flocks (18 km a day) takes about 2 days (urim travel). The margin of 3 days covers the packing and the gathering of the household, which the text does not time.

events.title: Israel offers sacrifices to the God of Isaac
events.narrative_summary: At Beersheba Israel offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the arrival at Beersheba ('and came to Beersheba, and offered', 46:1), so it starts at the end of the journey. A sacrificial service takes a few hours; the margin of a day allows for a rest before the offering, which the text does not mention.

events.title: God tells Jacob in a night vision not to fear going to Egypt
events.narrative_summary: God calls 'Jacob, Jacob' in a vision of the night, and Jacob answers. God says He is the God of his father, tells him not to fear going down to Egypt, promises to make him a great nation there, to go down with him and bring him up again, and that Joseph will close his eyes.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text says only 'in the visions of the night' (46:2) after the sacrifice. The night following the sacrifice is taken, snapped to the middle watch at 22:00 (offset 0 from the end of the sacrifice, so the first 22:00 at or after it). The margin of 4 hours reflects that the text names the night but no hour. The Targums (Onkelos 'in the visions of the night', Pseudo-Jonathan 'in prophecy in the night') add nothing about the time.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: In the visions of the night

events.title: Jacob's sons carry him and the household from Beersheba to Egypt
events.narrative_summary: Jacob rises from Beersheba and his sons carry him, their little ones and their wives in the wagons Pharaoh had sent, with their livestock and goods from Canaan. Jacob brings all his offspring with him into Egypt.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts after the vision (46:5 'And Jacob rose up from Beersheba'); the morning start is inferred (BOKER), the first morning after the night vision. Duration: Beersheba to Goshen is about 363 km by road; army mode for a caravan with wagons, children and flocks gives about 18 km a day, so about 20 days (urim travel; donkey mode would give 11 days, walking 12.5). The text states no duration. Margin of 1 day for the start; the tier is DAY_SEQUENCE since the text gives no time word.

events.title: Jacob sends Judah ahead to Joseph and they come into Goshen
events.narrative_summary: Jacob sends Judah ahead to Joseph to show the way before him to Goshen, and they come into the land of Goshen.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives no time for this. Judah goes ahead of the caravan, so he is placed in the final stretch of the journey: start 16 days after the departure, lasting 4 days, ending when the caravan reaches Goshen (46:28 'and they came into the land of Goshen'). The 4-day margin reflects that the point at which he was sent is unknown.

events.title: Joseph rides to Goshen, meets his father and weeps on his neck
events.narrative_summary: Joseph harnesses his chariot and goes up to Goshen to meet Israel his father. He appears to him, falls on his neck and weeps a long while. Israel says he can die now that he has seen Joseph's face and knows he is alive.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Anchored on the end of the caravan's journey, since the meeting is in Goshen when Jacob arrives; Joseph's own trip from his residence (Egypt to Goshen about 90 km, a chariot day at most) is covered by the margin of a day. An embrace and speech take a couple of hours. Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is given.

events.title: Joseph tells his family what to say to Pharaoh about their trade
events.narrative_summary: Joseph tells his brothers and his father's house that he will tell Pharaoh they have come. He instructs them to say, when Pharaoh asks their trade, that they have been keepers of livestock from their youth, so that they may live in Goshen, since shepherds are an abomination to the Egyptians.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A speech that follows directly on the meeting (46:31 'And Joseph said'), so it starts at the end of the meeting and takes about half an hour. The margin of 1 day allows that it may have been said later on the same journey to Goshen or the next day; the text marks no gap.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Pharaoh's wagons, sent with the brothers (45:19-21), are the means in which Jacob and the little ones are carried (46:5).
Having resolved to go and see Joseph before he dies (45:28), Israel sets out (46:1).
Now that his father's house has come to him in Goshen (46:29-31), Joseph must announce them to Pharaoh, so he tells them how to answer about their trade (46:31-34).
Judah goes ahead to Joseph to give directions to Goshen (46:28), so that Joseph can go up to meet his father there (46:29).
God's word 'fear not to go down into Egypt' (46:3-4) removes the hesitation and Jacob rises to go from Beersheba (46:5).

components.label_value: Promised a great nation in Egypt
components.evidence_explanation: 46:3 God says: do not fear to go down to Egypt, for I will make you a great nation there.

components.label_value: Arrived in the land of Goshen
components.evidence_explanation: 46:28 says they came into the land of Goshen; Joseph asks that they dwell there (46:34), and the settlement itself is granted later (47:6).

components.label_value: Content to die after seeing Joseph
components.evidence_explanation: 46:30 Israel says he can die now that he has seen Joseph's face.
46:28 the party comes to Goshen, where Joseph wants them to settle (46:34).
46:32 and 46:34 Joseph tells them to say they have been men of livestock from their youth.

systems.name: Sacrificial meal offered to God
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Throughout the ancient Near East, sacrifices (zebahim) were slaughtered at an altar or sacred place and part was eaten by the worshippers, as a way of seeking the god's favour before an undertaking. The patriarchs offer them at places tied to earlier encounters.
rules_and_mechanics: The offerer slaughters an animal at a sanctuary or altar
Part is shared in a meal before the deity
It is made to the God of the family's ancestors
It is fitting before a journey or a decision

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph presents himself to his father, falls on his neck and weeps a long time.
system_instances.significance_note: It ends the long separation and prompts Israel's wish to die now that Joseph lives.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God calls 'Jacob, Jacob' in the visions of the night and Israel answers 'Here I am'.
system_instances.significance_note: The reply to the doubled call, as in Gen 22 and Ex 3, shows readiness; the vision makes the descent to Egypt something God commands.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God promises to make Jacob a great nation in Egypt, to go down with him and bring him up again, and says Joseph will close his eyes.
system_instances.significance_note: It renews the covenant promise of nationhood in a foreign land and promises a return, linking the descent to the exodus.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Israel offers sacrifices at Beersheba to the God of his father Isaac before going down to Egypt.
system_instances.significance_note: Beersheba is where Isaac met God; the sacrifice asks for guidance at the first step outside the promised land.

edges.description: God tells Jacob not to be afraid of going down to Egypt.
God promises to make Jacob a great nation in Egypt and to bring him up again.
Israel offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac at Beersheba.
Jacob sends Judah ahead to Joseph to direct the way to Goshen.
Joseph falls on his father's neck and weeps for a long while.
Joseph tells his brothers to say they are men of livestock when Pharaoh asks their occupation.
Pharaoh sends wagons to carry Jacob and his household to Egypt.
The sons of Israel carry their father Jacob, with the children and wives, in Pharaoh's wagons.
